title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

reading.body:
This is an insider misuse of a deployed surveillance system, not a failure of the model or the hardware. The license plate readers did what they were built to do, returning location data on plates, and the failure sits at the query layer, where a police chief ran searches for a personal purpose rather than a police one. The system was used outside the conditions it was built for, and the person doing it held the authority to run those searches.

The conduct ran from June to October 2023, which means it was repeated across months rather than a single lapse. Catching it would have required the deployment to keep a reviewable record of who searched which plate and why, and for someone other than the searching officer to compare those queries against actual cases. A query log alone would not have stopped it, since the searches were authorised at the account level, but it would have made the pattern visible while it was happening.

What is not established is the exact number of searches, since the headline and the certification order give different figures, and no criminal charge or court finding appears in the reporting. The certification order is a finding by a state body about a police certification, and the account of the chief's admitted jealousy comes from that order.

reports.title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

summary: According to a Kansas certification order, Sedgwick, Kansas, Police Chief Lee Nygaard reportedly used Flock Safety license plate readers 228 times from June to October 2023 to check where his ex-girlfriend and her new boyfriend were. The order said he also followed them in a police vehicle and admitted jealousy influenced his conduct. Nygaard resigned in October 2023 and later lost his police certification.
